descriptionChirho: To be without something needed or expected; to have an insufficient amount of something, whether material possessions, spiritual gifts, or inherent qualities. The subject experiences a deficit in some respect. Arabic يَنْقُص/تَنْقُصون (lack/be deficient), Hebrew חָסֵר/חֲסֵרִים (lacking), Hindi कम–है/घटी (deficient/lacking), Korean 부족하다 (be insufficient), Spanish falta/carecer (lack/be without). Found across diverse contexts: the rich young ruler asking 'what do I lack?' (Matt 19:20, Mark 10:21), the disciples' lack during mission (Luke 22:35), all falling short of God's glory (Rom 3:23), lacking no spiritual gift (1 Cor 1:7), not lacking in food (1 Cor 8:8), the less honored body part (1 Cor 12:24), and knowing both abundance and lack (Phil 4:12).

To fail to reach or attain a goal, standard, or expectation; to come behind or be inferior to a benchmark. While related to 'lack,' this sense emphasizes the gap between an actual state and an expected standard rather than simple absence of a resource. Arabic نَقَصْتُ (I fell short), Hebrew לֹא–חָסַרְתִּי (I did not fall short -- negated), Hindi घटा–होना/पीछे–रह–जाए (to have fallen/to fall behind), Korean 모자라지–않았다 (not fallen short), Spanish haber–sido–inferior/quedando-atrás (to have been inferior/falling behind). Used of Paul's not being inferior to the 'super-apostles' (2 Cor 11:5, 12:11), the warning against falling short of entering God's rest (Heb 4:1), and failing to obtain the grace of God (Heb 12:15).

To experience privation or hardship due to lack of material necessities; to be in a state of neediness or destitution. This goes beyond simple deficiency to describe an existential condition of poverty and suffering. Arabic يَحْتَاج/مُحْتاجاً/مُعْوَزِينَ (need/needy/destitute), Hindi तंगी–में–रहने/तंग–भोगते (living in hardship/suffering distress), Korean 궁핍하다 (be destitute), Spanish padecer-necesidad/necesitados (suffer need/needy). Found in the parable of the prodigal son who 'began to be in need' (Luke 15:14), Paul's experience of want while preaching (2 Cor 11:9), and the faith heroes who went about 'destitute, afflicted, mistreated' (Heb 11:37).

Of a supply or resource: to become exhausted or depleted, to fail or run short. This sense is impersonal, applied to a commodity rather than a person, distinguishing it from the personal senses of lacking or being in need. Arabic لَمَّا–نَفِدَ (when it ran out/was exhausted), Hebrew כְּשֶׁחָסֵר (when it was lacking), Hindi कम–होने–पर (upon becoming less), Korean 떨어졌을–때 (when it fell/ran out), Spanish habiendo-faltado (having been lacking). The sole NT occurrence is at the wedding in Cana (John 2:3) where the wine ran out, prompting Jesus' first miracle. The genitive absolute construction (ὑστερήσαντος οἴνου) marks this as a distinct impersonal-supply usage.
